#4401. Tomorrow’s Battlefield 6 patch is the first step towards improving footstep audio, and it might actually fix the settings reset bug

The next major Battlefield 6 patch is nearly upon us, and Battlefield Studios is promising a bounty of changes - including a couple of fixes to some big bugs.

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew new content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#4400. Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space

For the first time, a robot has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without astronauts, demonstrating a technology that could dramatically change how large spacecraft and scientific instruments are built.

The robotic system was developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). It is part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, an initiative exploring ways to manufacture and assemble enormous structures directly in space.

Rather than relying on astronauts to connect individual pieces, the robot uses an automated arm to retrieve structural tubes and connecting joints from nearby storage dispensers. It then joins the components into repeating sections, called bays, that form a larger supporting framework known as a truss.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," says Sergio Pellegrino, the Joyce and Krent Kresa Professor of Aerospace and Civil Engineering, the Lynn Booth and Kent Kresa Department of Aerospace Leadership Chair, the executive officer for aerospace, and a senior research scientist at JPL, which Caltech manages for NASA.

A Historic Step Toward Building Giant Structures in Space

Pellegrino leads Caltech's Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA) demonstration. The robotic system has spent six months in orbit attempting to construct a reflector antenna measuring 1.4 meters across. Its design combines composite fiber tubes, aluminum connectors, and a lightweight reflective surface made from Kapton, a durable polymer film commonly used in spacecraft.

DARPA compares the assembly process to building with sophisticated versions of K'Nex or Tinkertoy construction toys. However, making a robot perform those same tasks reliably in the harsh environment of space presents a far greater engineering challenge.

The team encountered technical difficulties and scheduling constraints that prevented it from finishing the entire antenna. Nevertheless, the robot successfully assembled an initial section, providing evidence that this construction method can work in orbit. Researchers believe the same basic approach could eventually support much larger frameworks carrying enormous reflective surfaces.

The orbital experiment represents the third stage of DARPA's research program. During the first two stages, Caltech researchers developed the construction concept, worked out the engineering design, and verified its operation in laboratory experiments on Earth. The team then had less than 12 months to manufacture, test, and deliver the space hardware to Momentus Inc., the company hosting the payload.

"Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," says Pellegrino, who is also co-director of the Space Solar Power Project, which aims to harvest solar power in space and wirelessly transmit it to Earth's surface. "As we wrap up the mission, we are finally able to start thinking about the new avenues of research opened by this demonstration."

Why Scientists Want to Build Enormous Structures in Orbit

The ability to assemble large structures directly in space could transform astronomy, communications, and space based energy systems.

For example, future telescopes could use enormous reflective surfaces to collect more light and observe extremely distant objects. Similar structures could also support powerful radio antennas, allowing scientists and engineers to build communications systems much larger than those that can currently be launched.

One of the greatest obstacles is the limited room available inside a rocket's fairing, the protective enclosure that surrounds its payload during launch. No matter how ambitious a spacecraft design might be, its components must somehow fit inside that confined space.

Traditionally, engineers have addressed this problem in two ways. They either fold large structures into compact packages that can unfold after reaching orbit, or they launch separate components and have astronauts assemble them in space. Both approaches impose practical limits on the size and complexity of the finished structure.

Robotic construction offers a third possibility. Instead of fitting an enormous telescope or antenna inside a rocket, engineers could transport its materials into orbit and assemble the complete system there.

DARPA's Plan for Kilometer-Scale Space Structures

DARPA established NOM4D in 2022 to investigate technologies that could eventually "ferry raw materials from Earth for in-orbit manufacturing," according to the program's website.

Caltech's ASTRA experiment is one of only two projects selected to advance to the program's third phase, which involves demonstrating construction technologies in orbit.

The other project, led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, will use a module attached to the International Space Station to investigate a technique for hardening carbon tubes in space. This could provide another way to manufacture structural components without having to complete every step on Earth.

"NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," said Andrew Detor, DARPA program manager for NOM4D, in a written statement. "By 'very large,' I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today."

Such structures could eventually be several football fields long or even extend for kilometers, far beyond the dimensions of conventional spacecraft.

How Caltech's Construction Robot Reached Space

ASTRA began its journey on March 30, 2026, when a SpaceX Transporter-16 mission launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California early that morning.

The robot traveled aboard Momentus Inc.'s Vigoride 7 orbital vehicle, which carried 10 separate payloads into low Earth orbit. ASTRA occupied approximately one cubic meter of space, a compact package containing both the assembly machinery and the materials required for construction.

Inside were two previously assembled truss bays, reinforced with diagonal tubes and connecting joints. The payload also included a robotic arm and motorized dispensers loaded with the parts needed to construct the remaining sections.

The successful launch was an emotional moment for the small engineering team watching from Earth. Jaden Suh, a former Caltech postdoctoral scholar who is now an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin, was moved to tears as the spacecraft carrying his team's work headed into orbit.

"As a child, I was super curious about and interested in space structures. Just like many other engineers working in this field, sending your stuff to space is what I've been dreaming of my entire life," Suh says. "I was extremely lucky to have the opportunity to work on this project, beginning from scratch. A lot of my original ideas are included in this system, and it was just incredible seeing it reach space."

Building a Structure Hundreds of Miles Above Earth

After ASTRA reached orbit, researchers began operating the system by transmitting instructions to its onboard computer through the Vigoride spacecraft.

The initial steps involved releasing the mechanisms that had secured the components during launch. The robot then extended the two previously assembled truss bays out of the machine and proceeded to construct a third bay using the onboard assembly system.

Three team members managed the construction commands from Earth: Charles Sommer, a former Caltech systems engineer; Alan Truong, a Caltech research engineer; and graduate student Tara Venkatadri (MS '24).

Although the robot carried out the assembly operations automatically, the researchers monitored its progress using photographs transmitted from orbit. When something went wrong, they examined the images, adjusted their instructions, and attempted the operation again.

These setbacks were an important part of learning whether the technology could function outside a controlled laboratory.

"That's basically the reason you do proof-of-concept testing. There are a lot of differences in the space environment compared to down on Earth," Suh explains. "There are always lots of little surprises."

To diagnose problems in orbit, the engineers relied on a second ASTRA system kept at Pellegrino's laboratory at Caltech. This backup unit, known as a flight spare, allowed researchers to recreate difficulties encountered by the spaceborne robot and experiment with possible solutions.

"Every time we confirm there is an issue in space, we come to the laboratory and try to mimic the problem on the ground," Sommer says.

Communication restrictions made troubleshooting especially challenging. The team could contact ASTRA only during approximately seven or eight brief periods each day, with each opportunity lasting about 15 minutes.

That meant engineers had to make the most of their limited communication windows. They used the laboratory twin to investigate problems, evaluate different solutions, and determine which adjustments were most likely to work. Once a solution was ready, they sent the revised instructions to the robot in orbit.

This process helped the team work through numerous unexpected difficulties while gathering valuable information about what future autonomous construction systems will need to operate more reliably.

ASTRA's intended construction process involves repeating a carefully coordinated series of movements.

First, the robotic arm retrieves structural components from their storage dispensers. It positions the tubes and joints on an assembly plate and connects them to create a new truss bay.

Once the framework is assembled, the robot is designed to attach a thin reflective film containing many tiny openings. This material forms two reflective cable nets that are held under tension against one another by springs, helping the resulting surface maintain its intended shape.

The special film was jointly invented by researchers at Caltech and the University of Pennsylvania, where the collaborating team was led by Professor Igor Bargatin.

Unlike the knitted metallic mesh typically used in reflectors designed to fold and unfold, the perforated film requires less tension to maintain its shape. That allows engineers to reduce the amount of supporting structure needed, potentially making the entire assembly substantially lighter.

Lower weight is especially valuable in space engineering because every additional kilogram increases the demands placed on a launch vehicle.

When a bay is finished and its reflective components have been prepared, the robotic system pushes the completed section outward into space. It then begins assembling the next bay.

The full ASTRA antenna design calls for 11 connected bays, each attached to the reflective nets and extended outward from the assembly system.

A Small Demonstration With Enormous Implications

Despite successfully demonstrating the construction technique, the researchers do not expect ASTRA to finish assembling all 11 bays before the mission concludes in December.

The experiment has revealed several ways the robotic hardware and assembly procedure could be simplified and improved. Even without a completed antenna, the team believes it has collected enough evidence to establish that the approach is technically feasible.

The implications extend well beyond the relatively small antenna used in this demonstration.

Future robotic construction systems could help scientists build gigantic space telescopes that collect more light, radio antennas capable of supporting advanced communications, and enormous solar arrays designed to capture sunlight in orbit.

Such solar power systems could potentially transmit collected energy wirelessly to receivers on Earth, an idea being explored through Caltech's Space Solar Power Project.

More broadly, the successful test suggests that the size of future space infrastructure may not always have to be dictated by the dimensions of the rockets used to launch its components.

"Once you get to the size limit where structures cannot be prebuilt on the ground and unfolded, you have to think about how to build them in space," Pellegrino says. "So, this work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power."

#4397. Battlefield 6's latest update dubbed the game's simultaneously best and worst patch as it runs into all kinds of issues

What's likely going to be the last major Battlefield 6 update of the year has launched with a number of unexpected issues.

There’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical issues, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The issue remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer said it’s working on a proper fix.

Perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to quickly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

But Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the new Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

It’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many issues at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

#4396. 8 Best Anime Where Tiny Details Become Major Story Revelations

Usama Mehmood is a Senior Writer at DualShockers with more than five years of experience in the video game industry. He has been writing professionally since 2021 and covering games since 2022, with work spanning guides, lists, reviews, and features across action-adventure games, JRPGs, open-world titles, racing games,

You know, I’ve rewatched certain anime scenes more times than I’d like to admit on YT or just browsing social media, and it's almost never for the big moments. It’s usually for something small: a character’s hand hovering a half-second too long or a line of dialogue that sounded like filler. Then, twenty episodes later, the show unexpectedly turns that one detail into the thing that rewrites almost everything you thought you knew about it.

Watched These Once? These 8 Anime Hit Harder the Second Time Around

It’s like that foreshadowing or missing puzzle piece coming back later that just makes you bewildered for a second or two at the show’s ingenious attention-to-detail, or, well, certain parts of it, to be exact. It made rewatches feel like detective work, and it also makes you appreciate how much patience and planning go into a story that pays off its smallest choices.

So this anime list is for the shows that reward that kind of attention, especially the ones where you can catch the smallest details and understand why they become so prevalent later, during the climax. Naturally, there are lots of spoilers ahead for the discussed anime, so watch out!

It’s funny that I recommended this show to a friend who went into Higurashi expecting a wholesome slice-of-life show, only to regret trusting my recommendation. It's a horror show that takes some characters’ quirks and uses them as pivotal anchors in later episodes.

Take the first arc, for instance: when Keiichi starts scratching his throat, you get the impression that it's a nervous habit. A few arcs later, you realize it’s the first symptom of the Hinamizawa Syndrome, which explains why people who were perfectly friendly suddenly turn on each other.

The twins are another example. See, you know Mion and Shion Sonozaki look nearly identical, and the show plays with that on purpose, but once you know how the identity swap works, you start to doubt every earlier scene where “Mion” seemed slightly off. I can get why some people think this show is straight-up torture, but don’t knock it till you try, am I right?

Let me preface this by saying we don’t argue between Aronofsky’s Black Swan and Satoshi Kon’s Perfect Blue; I love both. This cult-favorite anime movie’s best trick is how it plays with your sense of what’s real. Mima’s decision to quit her pop group CHAM! and become an actress feels like a simple career move, but as you watch, the film shows how every “step forward” she takes strips away a piece of her.

The tiny, uneasy moments, like her flinching at the fax of the Double Bind script or the way her reflection starts reacting a half-beat late, are the film silently telling you that Mima isn’t in control of her own image anymore. And that’s one of the key reasons I adore this movie, even after all these years since I first watched it.

These anime plot twists flipped entire stories on their heads.

On a first watch, Madoka Magica looks like a bright, pastel magical girl series… until you rewatch it and realize it was telling you exactly how it would break your heart from the very first episode. Almost everything in the show, from the unusual designs of the Witch's Labyrinths to the seemingly innocent conversations with Kyubey, carries far more meaning than it initially lets on to you.

I mean, for crying out loud, the show's opening, with its seemingly disconnected imagery and Madoka chasing after a mysterious figure, becomes much more meaningful once you understand what's really happening. Even small character choices carry weight. Mami’s tea parties, her loneliness, and her insistence on keeping up the cheerful senpai act are all easy to read as charm early on in this show.

Now I’ll be very real with you all here; Odd Taxi looks like a quiet slice-of-life show about a walrus cab driver named Hiroshi Odokawa, and it’s hard to say anything about it without spoiling it. He’s a dry, awkward man who talks in deadpan dad jokes and likes listening to a comedy podcast between fares.

Then a missing girl, a yakuza fixer, an idol group, a struggling comedian, and a nurse with a secret all begin orbiting his cab. What looks like a pile of unrelated conversations turns out to be a tightly built puzzle, and almost every piece of it was planted in the very first episodes.

Early on, much of the dialogue feels like filler, with passengers rambling about their lives or Odokawa making small talk, until you later realize this throwaway stuff sets up most of the plot because a casual remark about a missing person, an offhand comment about someone’s job, or even a name dropped once in passing can fill in the main structure of the mystery. The show trusts you to notice, and it rewards you.

Dive into anime with controversial endings with modern shockers like Death Note and classics such as Evangelion.

Everyone knew this was going to be here, and it deserves it even if it's an obvious pick for this list. Death Note is an anime practically built around the idea that the smallest details can make the biggest difference.

What starts as a straightforward cat-and-mouse game between Light and L quickly becomes an elaborate battle of deduction, manipulation, and psychological warfare, where a seemingly insignificant action can expose someone's entire plan.

Whether it's L noticing the peculiarities of Kira's early killings or Light carefully manipulating the Death Note’s rules, the show constantly rewards those who pay attention. It's incredibly satisfying to watch everything click into place, and while the latter half isn’t everyone’s favorite for obvious reasons, the finale is genuinely one of the most memorable endings in the entire anime medium.

I might be biased for including this because Steins;Gate is genuinely one of my favorite anime of all time, and just a few months ago in August, I had the chance to review the Steins;Gate Reboot VN—and the entire thing was just as good as I remembered.

It starts as a quirky science-fiction adventure about a group of eccentric friends experimenting with a microwave, then accidentally stumbles into a conspiracy-theory time-travel adventure that gradually becomes one of the most intricately woven narratives in the medium. I know that sounds like a mouthful, but anyone who’s seen the show will know the series is just like that in terms of writing.

The genius is in how casually the show introduces certain characters, conversations, messages, and seemingly throwaway moments before revealing just how important they are to the bigger picture at the very end, or just when a certain pocket watch strikes 7:35 PM. Sorry, had to do it.

Look, we’re not even going to get into the debate about how the show ended, so this will focus strictly on Attack on Titan’s brilliant foreshadowing, which led to major story revelations and more twists, as my listicle’s title already suggests.

No matter what you think of his directional choices for the last act, Isayama has an incredible knack for planting seemingly insignificant details throughout the story. Things like the truth behind the Walls, the mystery surrounding Eren's basement, and the peculiar behavior of certain Titans initially seem like separate mysteries, but eventually come together in ways that completely change your understanding of the world in later seasons.

Even ordinary moments in both the manga and anime involving characters like Reiner, Bertholdt, and Annie become far more interesting once you pay attention to their behavior or dialogue, since they ultimately foreshadow their twists.

Naoki Urasawa is one of the most legendary manga auteurs with a wide range of back-to-back bangers under his umbrella, but his work in Monster is honestly one of the best things you’ll ever get to see, as long as you’re patient enough.

This slow-burn psychological thriller is the kind of story where an innocent conversation or a character's seemingly insignificant memory can carry far more weight than you initially realize. Even some of the twists thrown in here at times can recontextualize things you've already witnessed in previous episodes, making them feel completely different when you look back at them.

The mystery surrounding Johan, the Kinderheim 511 experiments, and the disturbing picture-book stories are all excellent examples of how Urasawa plants little breadcrumbs throughout the narrative before gradually revealing their significance.

From One Piece's grand treasure to Itachi's tragic illness, these unsolved anime mysteries leave fans guessing.

#4395. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."

Materials provided by Rockefeller University Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4393. Arc Raiders gets a few map exploit fixes in latest patch as Embark prepares to slow down how often patches are released

There's a new Arc Raiders patch that's fairly small, but one with fixes everyone is going to appreciate.

The time has arrived for another Arc Raiders update, and Embark has certainly delivered. Today’s patch, version 1.6.0, is among the smallest the game has received so far, focusing almost exclusively on disabling map exploits.

Perhaps more important than the patch itself, however, is the announcement the developer made around it.

Starting off with patch 1.6.0, it takes out a particular zipline on Stella Montis, the game’s most recent addition ot the map roster. Some players used said zipline to get out of bounds, something the game has been battling on several of its maps.

On Blue Gate, the patch fixes a collision issue that allowed players to vault through a wall, and fall to their death. The map fixes continue with another on Spaceport Launch Tower, which takes out a gap in collision that players have been able to shoot through.

The last change in this update affects gameplay feel around Arc enemies. Certain materials in the game’s world weren’t blocking their vision - or fire - when they should have, and this has now been fixed.

Alongside today’s patch, Embark also announced that going forward, we’re going to see fewer patches for Arc Raiders. The game has been getting updates almost every Thursday since it launched in late October.

Now that most of the major problems have been fixed, the studio is shifting to a slower patching cadence. Critical fixes will still be issued as soon as they’re developed, but don’t expect a patch each week going forward.

Embark also revealed that patch releases and in-game store rotations will now occur on Tuesdays. You should also expect the next few weeks to be quiet, as members of the team go on holiday breaks.

But, before everyone goes away, the game is going to get one more big update. The last item on Arc Raiders’ roadmap, revealed in early November, is the Cold Snap event. This is on track for Tuesday, bringing some new content alongside a few other fixes.

#4390. Dispatch's Anniversary Update Brings Commentary Track, Storyboard Mode, And Mobile Port

Dispatch, a superhero-themed workplace comedy from last year, celebrates its one-year anniversary today. While it was released episodically, the first batch dropped on October 22. It was received well, with strong performances from a star-studded cast (including Breaking Bad star Aaron Paul) and filled a niche left vacant by Telltale Games' absence from the gaming world in recent years. Today, developer AdHoc announced a batch of anniversary content, and some of it drops today.

First, there's a new way to play Dispatch: storyboard mode. This option lets you play through the whole experience using the original animatics – rough placeholder sketches that the artists used to sync images up to the voice-over. It's a fun behind-the-scenes look at the game's development that we don't get very often. In that same vein, the cast and crew recorded DVD-style commentary tracks to play over the game, making jokes and sharing insight into the development process. A press release says there are over 16 hours of commentary from the game's development team (like art director Derek Stratton and creative directors Dennis Lenart and Nick Herman) as well as some of the cast, including Aaron Paul, Laura Bailey, and Erin Yvette.

Storyboard and Commentary modes are included in the game's deluxe edition, which you can upgrade to for $10.99. Both modes are available today.

If you haven't played the game yet, AdHoc has announced a new way to do so; Dispatch is coming to mobile platforms on December 9. It's been rebuilt to support touch controls and vertical play, and it will be available on iOS and Android. You can even play the first half of the game for free – the first four episodes are included, but you'll need to pay $19.99 to play the rest.

Finally, AdHoc announced new merch, including a book created alongside publisher Lost in Cult called Dispatch: Design Works, which is both an art book and a "making-of" book. There's also a live game soundtrack concert in Los Angeles featuring Thot Squad, Bershy, Primer, Caroline Kingsbury, Fartbarf, and Dispatch composer Andrew Arcadi with the SDN Company Band. It will be held at Avalon Hollywood on December 3, but it won't be livestreamed, so you'll need to grab a ticket to see the event. The press release states that people who signed up for updates from adhocstudio.com will be the first in line to purchase tickets.

#4389. Gentle Mates GC come from a map down to beat Shopify Rebellion Gold and reach Game Changers final

Gentle Mates GC, on their Championship debut, beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo. The French-based side go into Sunday's best-of-five grand final with a two-map ban advantage, while Shopify Rebellion Gold must come through the lower final.

Gentle Mates GC are into the grand final of the VCT Game Changers Championship 2026. They beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo on Friday 30 October. The French-based side dropped the opening map and then took the next two. Both teams had arrived at the match with every map at the event won.

Shopify Rebellion Gold won map one, which lasted 53 minutes. On the second map they fought back to 10-10, but Gentle Mates closed it out 13-11 after 55 minutes. The decider on Summit ran for 57 minutes and finished 13-10 to Gentle Mates.

Coming through the upper bracket gives Gentle Mates a two-map ban advantage in the grand final. Shopify Rebellion Gold, led at the event by interim in-game leader alexis, drop into the lower bracket final against KRÜ Blaze.

This is Gentle Mates’ first appearance at the Championship. Their line-up of Marti, Nami, Wens, tokameite and berryx reached the upper final with 2-0 wins over Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. Their last three EMEA Stage 3 results before the event were wins over G2 Gozen and SK Nebula, both 2-1, and a 3-2 defeat to G2 Gozen.

The Elo power rankings already had Gentle Mates ahead. They sit fourth with a rating of 1844 and a 33-7 record from 40 rated matches. Shopify Rebellion Gold are sixth on 1809, with a 40-20 record from 60 rated matches.

Shopify Rebellion Gold had cleared SK Nebula and KRÜ Blaze without losing a map. Before travelling, they beat FlyQuest RED 3-1 and 2-1 and SwimTrek Blue 2-0 in North America Stage 2. At last year’s Championship in Seoul, Team Liquid Brazil beat them 3-2 in the title match.

The lower bracket final is a rematch. Shopify Rebellion Gold beat KRÜ Blaze in the upper semi-final. KRÜ then earned their place with lower bracket wins over Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC, both without dropping a map. MIBR GC finished fourth, which is worth $50,000. SK Nebula, one of three EMEA teams in São Paulo, placed joint fifth to sixth for $25,000. Their line-up included Scottish player fluxxy.

Third place pays $70,000. The lower bracket final and the grand final are both best-of-five, after best-of-three series in the earlier rounds of the double-elimination bracket. Ten teams entered the event at Riot Games Arena, which Riot describes as the last Game Changers Championship to be held as a standalone event. In 2027 the Championship moves to Austin, Texas. For the first time it will run in the same city at the same time as VALORANT Champions, from 16 September to 10 October.

Shopify Rebellion Gold and KRÜ Blaze meet in the lower bracket final on Saturday 31 October at 15:00 BRT. The winner faces Gentle Mates GC in the grand final on Sunday 1 November at 15:00 BRT.

#4388. The best soft launch mobile games for iPhone, iPad or Android

The biggest games yet to launch on the global market

If you've been looking for something new and exciting that isn't quite fully released, then look no further; you've found our list of the best games currently in soft launch.

Sometimes developers like to make sure the paying public is willing to play their game before they push it to every device in the world - that's where soft launch comes in. Available in just a handful of countries and regions, a soft-launched game is subject to drastic change as developers take on board customer feedback (and other metrics) to alter the game and ensure the best possible product is ready for when it goes to worldwide launch.

But here's the kicker - we can see when developers do that. And when you're looking at some of the big games, like the ones we have on this list, then you can find yourself getting very excited, and even a little jealous that you can't play them yet.

So to help you out a little, we've collected a huge list of some of the biggest and best games currently available in soft launch, which you might well be able to get if you have the right Apple ID or Google Play account to download them with.

Just as a note: In the case of a game suddenly disappearing, it might be because the developer has decided to stop development on it early and save themselves the cost of a big launch, or because the developer is gearing up for a big launch and wants to surprise the world. Whatever the case, we'll try to keep you updated when these things happen.

Let's get into the list! SoulTerra Odyssey

An interesting one here. Bandai Namco has dived back into the mobile world with a completely new IP. They're also claiming it's the first 'Match3D Roguelite Battle Game ever.' Given the sheer breadth of games out there, I highly doubt it, but it's an intriguing combination, nonetheless.

Sonic Rumble sees the blue blur returning to mobile, this time as a battle royale of sorts. In the mould of games like Stumble Guys and Fall Guys, it appears we can expect to dash around obstacle-filled courses, dodging the numerous hazards that threaten to eliminate us at every turn. It's definitely a setup that suits Sonic and co, but is it entering a market that's already been conquered by Scopely? Only time will tell.

Casual strategy games are all the rage these days, particularly on mobile. Anything that gives you a slight hit of feeling clever without requiring in-depth tactics that take forever to learn. Century Games' Crown of Bones is the latest attempt at sliding into that niche. It sees you joining the Skeleton King and his army as they battle through numerous realms. It sports a colourful art style that reminds me somewhat of little toy towns and villages, something you might have created in real life as a child, perhaps. As for the gameplay, it pretty much consists of increasing your numbers, upgrading your troops and toppling your opponents. There are a few special items thrown in for good measure as well.

If you're a football fan, you're probably already aware of Nordeus as the folks behind the popular management sim Top Eleven. With their latest effort, Top Goal, they are swapping the touchline for the pitch as you take direct control over your squad, having a more active role in the outcome of a match. Still, it seems some of the strategic side remains as you build your squad and choose your formation before taking on other players in PvP.

While it might seem as though the era of endless runners has passed on mobile, several still do very well, particularly if they have brand power behind them. Zapak hopes that Ben 10 Alien Run can join that list, putting a lot of stock in the popular children's cartoon pulling in the younger generation.

In it, you will dash around while transforming into one of nine different aliens, each bringing special abilities to the table. That might be creating a shield to block an enemy attack in one instance, while another might clear the path ahead with laser beams. On top of that, there are the usual daily challenges and missions you'd expect from the genre.

Oh My Anne is a match-3 game based on the popular novel series Anne of Green Gables. Players proceed through the story by completing levels and associated challenges. It's certainly interesting to see Neowiz deciding to take established, historical (1908~) novels and their IP and spin them off into games. There's a question to be asked about brand recognition and 'crossover IP' when those IPs are not ones from the current vogue. We regularly see Warhammer and Marvel crossover games, but those things are currently 'in', Anne of Green Gables — and Oh My Anne — targets a different audience and plays by different rules of advertising. Could there be a Dracula, Canterbury Tales or Beowulf games on the horizon if this takes off?

NetEase's Stumble Guys killer, Eggy Party, is rapidly moving toward its global release with seven new regions granted access to it in January of 2024; before that, it was simply in the SEA region. What's the big appeal? Well, if you're not sold by the constant party, cheerful colours and multiplayer mania of Eggy Party, then maybe the map creation will be the thing to grab your attention. A bumbling race to the finish might be fun, but doing it on a map that you - or one of your friends - created is vastly more fun.

Zynga, who you likely know for, well, many things, are working on a new addition to their growing merge catalogue. FruitFall – don't forget the double capital Fs – tasks you with merging fruits to beat each level. Simple, right? Judging by the store description, expect this to become more difficult as you progress. At first, it'll likely be a case of simply merging fruit, while the latter stages will introduce troublesome crates and frozen fruit that need thawing out before becoming useful. Zynga claims each level brings something different, keeping the challenge fresh and fun. Time will tell if that's the case

Mattel Match: Toybox looks to bring together the company's many toys under one roof, including Uno, Masters of the Universe and, of course, Barbie. How? You might ask. Through match-3 puzzling, that's how.

As you'll likely have guessed from the name, Puzzletown Mysteries sees you unravel mysteries by solving puzzles. There is also a town involved. The overarching whodunit is whether poor Gladys slipped from her balcony or if she received a little push before toppling over the edge, while you'll also look into a case of stolen cats.

As you've likely already guessed from the name, we're talking tower defence here. Here, the slight twist on the usual formula is that, alongside setting up your various defences, you'll actually build the map your enemies will march down. Of course, that's something we've seen before, but it's a fun twist nevertheless. I'm quite fond of the visuals, which have a super clean and easy-to-read look that's just shy of qualifying as minimalist.

Diamond Dreams is looking to bring a sense of elegance to the match-3 genre. The whole idea is that you're working towards crafting some stunning jewellery that, I have to say, looks far better than it possibly needs to.

Given the immense popularity of Monopoly Go, it seemed inevitable that similar games would pop up eventually. Coin Master – Board Adventure from Moon Active is one such attempt. Having already achieved success with Coin Master, I'd imagine this will also do incredibly well.

Cats & Soup has made a name for itself in recent times with its lovely aesthetic and focus on feline companions. While it's still a fairly familiar idle RPG, the focus on cosiness helped it stand out from a massive crowd. Evidently buoyed by its success, a spin-off called Cats & Soup: Magic Recipe is now in the works. Once again, the team are taking on a familiar mobile genre, bringing some warm-fuzzy cuteness to the merge-and-match realm. The aim is to cook delicious recipes, build a lovely home for your kitties, and make friends with new cats.

The humble match-3 will likely never lose popularity on mobile. It's simple to understand and great for playing on the go since it hits a nice spot between relaxing and engaging the brain. It's not surprising, then, that we often have big franchises delve into the genre. The latest to try their white-gloved hand is Disney with Disney Magic Match 3D. In it, you'll remove colourful clutter. No, really. Check out Catherine's preview to learn more.

While George R R Martin might have no interest in finishing his own book series, there is still plenty of Game of Thrones content to enjoy. Dragonfire is the latest, a tile-based strategy game that lets you put the titular fire-breathing winged beasties to work. But it's not simply sending them into battle. You will hatch and train them, taking your little fiery friend from a cute baby to a creature capable of barbecuing enemy villages.

We all love Fruit Ninja, but if there's one criticism you can throw its way, it's that it didn't have much else going for it beyond slicing up fruit. Adventure looks to change this by introducing a level-based approach that sees you solving puzzles alongside stabbing melons. You can also unlock new weapons and abilities as you progress, presumably allowing you to dice a kiwi in untold ways.

FairyTale Quest is a roguelite action RPG in the style of something like Vampire Survivors. And its characters? Well, as you've likely guessed, they're all pulled from traditional stories. So you can expect the Big Bad Wolf and Red Riding Hood to fight by your side. They can put aside their differences for the greater good, it seems.

That's right. Plants Vs Zombies 3 is back in soft launch, this time with Evolved after the colon. This refers to the merging mechanics they're throwing in with their latest attempt. We'll see how that all pans out in due course, but it's hard not to be a little sceptical given that EA has clearly struggled to figure out what they want to do with PvZ.

It's been almost ten years since Hill Climb Racing 2 launched, so it likely feels about time for a sequel for fans of wacky, physics-based driving. In the third instalment, you can expect plenty of special gadgets and handy boosts for increasing your performance on the bouncy track. There are also the plentiful customisation options on offer that any self-respecting racer needs. If we can't pimp our ride, what's the point?

Aside from the obvious flock and little green candy-loving monster, there are few games more iconic on mobile than Temple Run. That's why the announcement of a third has got us excited here at Pocket Gamer. But do those simple yet effective mechanics stand up after all these years, or are massive changes needed? Well, check out Catherine's Temple Run 3 preview to see what she thought.

Cute little penguins running around an obstacle course in Fall/Stumble Guys fashion? Haven't we already seen this with Pudgy Party? Apparently, Smilegate thinks they can do better, and personally, I'm all for it. Penguins are wonderful little creatures, and the more games where they're the star, the better. It sees you participating in 10-minute matches where the aim is to get your beak across the line first.

If you love pinging marbles and cutesy creatures, Marblebound might be the perfect fit for you. You gather a team of four heroes and then head into battle to take down a series of fearsome foes. And you'll do that by firing marbles at them, including ricocheting them off walls if you know your angles.

FunPlus, who you may know from State of Survival and DC: Dark Legion, among others, appears to be working on a new game. This one's called Dark Shot Survival and sees you building up a base to fend off night creatures (yes, they look like zombies to me, too). The whole thing seems to centre around a day/night cycle, wherein you spend the waking hours gathering resources and fortifying your base. Then, when the sun goes down, you'll need to fend off the zomb— sorry, night creatures, with all your might.

Angry Birds Rush sees Rovio's recognisable avians slinging themselves into a different genre. By the looks of things, Rush is an endless runner that sees you bouncing through various colourful locales all inspired by the series' many other games. It doesn't appear to be a straightforward runner, though, with slingshot elements still present to some extent.

There are few cartoon duos more iconic than Tom & Jerry. I'm not even a huge fan of them, but they'd certainly spring to mind if I had to name two long-standing cartoon rivals. It's that instant recognition that probably helped Steer Studios decide it was an IP worth working with. Tom and Jerry Blast is a puzzler that, based on the screenshots, sees you tapping your way through each level and using boosters if they ever become overly tricky.

You wouldn't necessarily put sailing the seven seas and tower defence together, but that's exactly what Puzala is going for with Stormborn Era. In it, you take charge of Black Sam and his crew, defending their ship from the hordes of enemies that have nothing better to do with their time than attack a big boat.

The Girls' Frontline series has proven incredibly popular over the years. Apparently, conventionally attractive women with guns will always do well. Who knew? Anyway, you can check out Catherine's Ahead of the Game to see if it's more than just a surface-level shooter.

Having briefly appeared in the US a while back, Borderlands Mobile has crept back into soft launch in Canada. The latest iteration has revealed that we can play as long-time fan-favourite Mad Moxxi, which I'm sure will be welcome news to many folks.

#4385. Tenebris Somnia Review – A Hair-Raising And Entertaining Throwback

Tenebris Somnia channels the old-school appeal of classic point-and-click adventures, survival horror, and full-motion-video (FMV) experiences, then smartly modernizes them to create a creepy, entertaining experience. Surviving the twisted threats of a demonic dream world is a tightly packed adventure that rewards you with what’s essentially an impressive indie horror film peppered throughout. It’s a nightmare you may not want to wake up from.

The blend of live-action and in-game storytelling works well in Tenebris Somina’s adventure, which begins when protagonist Julia visits the apartment of her filmmaker ex-boyfriend, Ivan, after suffering recurring nightmares of him being massacred by monsters. What begins as a well-meaning check-in on his status spirals down an unsettling rabbit hole when Julia’s worst fears are realized and then some. The dialogue-free tale presents a scary but fascinating exploration of obsession, both in art and in romance, that constantly delivers surprising, and at times upsetting, revelations during its eight-hour runtime. While Tenebris Somnia sometimes leans a little too far into “tell, don’t show” territory when explaining the cool lore of its supernatural threats, I never felt lost or confused about the wild things that regularly unfold on screen.

FMV experiences are nothing new, but Tenebris Somnia’s live-action scenes are a highlight. They’re well shot, sport impressively gruesome practical effects, and even present visual clues that make them important to gameplay. These scenes are additive, never taking too much time away from the in-game action, and they feel well placed to elicit the strongest emotional response. I also appreciate how the live scenes fit thematically, as much of Tenebris Somnia’s tale centers on a horror film shot by Ivan and Julia that significantly impacted their former relationship; at times, it’s like watching a movie about the movie. While I enjoy smaller moments, like opening a door to trigger a live-action jump scare, the filmmaking succeeds in selling Julia's emotions and the cast's reactions. Seeing real fear, concern, and determination in Julia’s eyes as she navigates a dreamworld made up of Ivan’s memories helped endear me to what would otherwise be a featureless pixel sprite.

Gameplay may look unimpressive due to its old-school adventure game presentation, but Tenebris Somnia’s spin on familiar survival-horror mechanics hits the right notes. Taking place entirely within a dreamlike version of a four-story apartment building, you’ll traverse floors collecting and combining objects and deciphering clues to solve well-crafted puzzles. I’m impressed by how well the game’s puzzles make the most of its limited graphical presentation, including clever scenarios involving mirror/screen reflections I won’t spoil, and how consistently creative they are. One devious exercise even utilizes the game’s limited save points as an unexpected resource in a way that changes how you approach your adventure going forward. No matter how strange puzzles become, they are never opaque, requiring just enough out-of-the-box thinking to make me feel smart when I connect the dots.

Battling grotesque monsters (which, naturally, look even creepier in live-action) also feels good, with melee and gunplay sporting deliberate animations reminiscent of classic adventure games without feeling mechanically clunky. Taking on multiple enemies by swinging a pipe or blowing them away with a shotgun feels better than it looks, and the most intense encounters end just as they approach the line of becoming overwhelming.

Boss battles, perhaps most unexpectedly for a largely puzzle-focused adventure, are fun and distinct from each other, be it wave-based bouts against small gremlin-like foes, protecting a fragile effigy of yourself from a parade of demented house servants, or battling literal mirror images of a tentacled flesh monster the Resident Evil series would be proud to claim. Managing limited ammo and health strikes a good balance of feeling tense but not oppressive. Playing conservatively is rewarding, as few non-boss threats need to be engaged if you can evade them well enough. But when I did find myself down to my last bullet or on the verge of death, Tenebris Somnia lets you feel the pinch just long enough before dropping a box of bullets or a health vial at the right moment.

Tenebris Somnia mines the enjoyable nostalgia of playing the horror games of yesteryear without feeling dated in the worst way. Weaving a solid indie horror film adds to the experience rather than feeling like a gimmick. The result is a captivating, well-executed survival-horror romp that maintains a hair-raising atmosphere with a fraction of the pixels of other genre giants.

#4384. Diablo 4's next expansion is bringing two new classes to the game, one of which you can play right now

Lord of Hatred may finally make good on the Mephisto arc of Diablo 4's campaign, which started in the original game and carried through Vessel of Hatred.

Very much when we expected it, Blizzard has officially revealed Diablo 4’s next major expansion at The Game Awards. Lord of Hatred delivers a new campaign that continues the mainline story, picking up from where Vessel of Hatred left off. Mephisto, the eponymous Lord of Hatred, has seemingly finally escaped imprisonment to rule over Sanctuary.

Lord of Hatred is the second Diablo 4 expansion, and it will be available on PC, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S on April 28.

It’s always a big deal when we get a new Diablo expansion, especially for a game as starved of fresh (major) content as Diablo 4 has been. But perhaps the biggest piece of news out of the Lord of Hatred reveal is that the expansion is bringing not one, but two new classes to the game.

The first of which is The Paladin, whereas the second is being kept under wraps. Even more surprising is that The Paladin is playable right now for anyone who pre-purchases the expansion. This is a well-timed shadow drop, especially given that Diablo 4’s latest season has just kicked off.

The expansion adds a new region to the world: Skovos, which is where the events of the new campaign will be taking place. This is the first time Skovos has been in a Diablo game. The region is of major significance to the world and lore of the series, as it is the birthplace of the firstborn, home of Lilith and Inaruis.

Lord of Hatred brings a decent number of major systems to Diablo 4. The endgame is getting a big overhaul, headlined by the new War Plans feature. Through this, you can effectively design your own endgame grind, creating challenges based on the activities you like and earning rewards along the way.

Endgame activities now also feature their own skill trees, which can be progressed through by creating War Plans for your character featuring each activity. The new endgame activity, Echoing Hatred, is something of horde mode where you must defend against unrelenting waves of enemies.

None of that matters without loot, of course, and the upcoming expansion is bringing back the Horadric Cube, and adding set bonuses using the Talisman system. The long-awaited and highly-requested Loot Filter is also coming to the game with the release of the expansion.

Beyond itemisation, each class’ skill tree will grow with new bonus skill variants. In fact, the entire skill system is being reworked for all classes - though details are a little sparse at the moment.

You can also expect the level cap to go up, which is very likely necessary to fit all the new skills and various systems. Blizzard offered a deep dive into the new Paladin class, which you see on the official blog.

#4382. The highly-anticipated follow-up to Baldur's Gate 3 is more Divinity, but it's not technically Original Sin 3

Larian has returned to tease a grand vision for its next major project, a new Divinity.

Larian Studios has delivered what was arguably the biggest reveal of The Game Awards 2025 showcase. The Hellstone, the mysterious monolith in the desert that’s been generating a lot of speculation in the lead-up to the show was indeed teasing the studio’s next game.

The Belgian developer is returning to the series it created with Divinity, a non-numbered sequel that’s designed for new and veteran players alike. The announcement was entirely cinematic, setting the tone for what looks to be the next big thing in the space.

Larian calls Divinity its most ambitious title ever, with the studio striving for a level of depth and breadth we’ve not seen before. This is the next project from the Baldur’s Gate 3 team, after all, so there’s understandably immense anticipation for it.

Divinity is a standalone RPG, and does not require you to have played Divinity: Original Sin, or Divinity: Original Sin 2. If you did, however, you’re going to find the journey extra special because of the continuity it offers.

“We’re ready to bring everything we’ve done previously into one place,” said founder and game director, Swen Vincke.

“This marks the beginning of something with more breadth, depth, and intimacy than anything we’ve created before. We’ve been building toward this moment ever since we took our fate into our own hands. This is the Divinity we’ve always wanted to make and you're going to have loads of fun with it.”

Beyond that, there’s precious little that’s been revealed for Divinity so far. We don’t know what platforms it’s going to be coming to, nor do we even have a release target. We do know it’s an RPG, so you can very much expect something similar to earlier games in the series, and, of course, Baldur’s Gate 3.

#4381. A Mass Effect 5 Trailer Featuring Liara Appears To Have Leaked Following BioWare's Closure

In case you missed the tragic news yesterday, EA laid off 400 employees this week, including all of BioWare. The studio behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and more, has been shut down, and its last remaining project was canceled. The game in question was a fifth entry in the Mass Effect universe, and BioWare shared very little about it – not even an official name. Following the studio's closure, however, a trailer for the sci-fi sequel started circulating around the internet.

While no official BioWare representatives have confirmed that the footage is real, Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier claims that it is. Schreier has a history of credible reporting in the field, and was the first to break the news about the layoffs. IGN has also stated that it confirmed the trailer's legitimacy.

If you want to see for yourself, you can watch the trailer on Reddit.

"The following is in-engine footage form our small team," text at the start of the video reads. "It uses our pre-production assets." The footage shows no gameplay, but includes a good-looking CG cutscene of a new protagonist speaking with an asari woman in a crowded bar. As he tells her about his life, we see glimpses of him as a soldier, then as some kind of spy, traveling to several planets to track down conflicts and "stopping them before they start." After the asari woman reveals that she's been "starting the fires" he's trying to prevent, another woman behind her lowers a hood. This new woman reveals herself as Liara T'Soni, one of Mass Effect's most iconic characters.

Then, Liara and the protagonist team up to take out the woman at the bar and her henchmen, using guns and telekinetic abilities. The trailer fades to black, then fades back in to reveal the game's would-be title: Mass Effect Universe. It's a great-looking trailer – it's a shame the game will never see the light of day.

If you want to join us in grieving BioWare, we republished an oral history of the studio that was originally written by former editor Matt Bertz in 2016. #4380. Every Pokémon Gimmick, Ranked

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

Over the years, we have seen many different Pokémon gimmicks pop up. It seems like every generation of Pokémon needs to have its own gimmick to make it stand out from the others.

It has come to a point where many fans of the series are tired of seeing new gimmicks pop up, and they would rather Pokémon go back to its roots with simple turn-based battles.

Unfortunately, that is never going to be the case, so you must accept whatever gimmick is in each game. Some of these gimmicks aren’t bad, but other ones are rather questionable. Let’s compare each of these gimmicks and see how they stack up against each other.

After introducing Mega Evolutions to Pokémon, Game Freak needed something to top it. Unfortunately, the gimmick in the next games, Sun and Moon, ended up being what is considered the worst gimmick in the Pokémon series.

The gimmick in question is Z-Moves. Z-Moves allow your Pokémon to use a massively powerful move, provided they are holding the appropriate Z-Crystal. Many have said that requiring an item to use one all-powerful move is a bit lame.

These all-powerful moves are often viewed as the one-hit option, allowing you to clear battles easily without much strategy being involved. The gimmick often felt unbalanced, and the addition of annoying, unskippable cutscenes, made using the moves extremely annoying.

I am someone who absolutely loves the Paldea region. I think that it is a beautiful area, and the idea that battles are celebrated in massive arenas is actually really cool to me. However, this generation of Pokémon games has one of the worst gimmicks, and that is Dynamaxing.

Dynamaxing allows a Pokémon to grow massive, amplifying its power in the process, and giving it access to different moves. In theory, it sounds decent. However, it is a nightmare for competitive play, as it makes already extremely powerful Pokémon even more powerful instead of lifting up and helping weaker Pokémon.

In addition to this, the moves given to the Pokémon are not unique, as they become different moves based on the previous move’s type, so a flying-type move will always become the same move when Dynamaxed. There are even more issues with it, but it all boils down to the gimmick feeling like not much thought went into it, as it is rather unbalanced and makes battles a bit of a slog.

Our picks for the best Pokémon Champions teams that are sure to help you climb this season.

If you were around for the Ruby and Sapphire days of Pokémon, then you remember double battles. These changed the way that Pokémon battles were played, and then they were expanded on in a rather weird way when triple Battles and rotational Battles appeared in Pokémon Black and White.

These battle types have rarely appeared since their inception, and it is because they weren’t very popular at the time. Triple battles are simple, involving three Pokémon being on the field at once instead of two. This is a bit unnecessary, as double battles were already fine.

Additionally, rotational battles were annoying because you had the ability to rotate your Pokémon around whenever you wanted, making some moves completely obsolete. However, it did make things interesting because the mechanic of rotating your Pokémon was different from switching them in and out of battle.

Terastallization is a gimmick that has the fanbase rather mixed, as there are many who enjoy the mechanic, and then there are those who absolutely hate it. As far as things go, it is a rather middle-of-the-road gimmick that could have been better, but it isn’t that bad.

This gimmick, which was introduced in Pokémon Scarlet and Violet, allows you to crystalize your Pokémon, changing its typing in the process. Many enjoy the mechanic because it lets you change the Pokémon’s typing, making them more resistant to moves they were once weak against.

The argument against Terastallization is that it can be unbalanced in certain battle formats, but it is mostly a balanced mechanic that works well with the series. The other argument is that every Pokémon looks absolutely terrible when it Terastalizes, and to be honest, they aren’t wrong.

Whether they're unlikely or just silly, these are the Ridiculous Pokémon Mega Evolutions We Would Love To See.

As stated earlier in the article, double battles were introduced in Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire, and they have remained to this day. It is one of the few earlier gameplay gimmicks that people sometimes forget started as a gimmick because it was so beloved.

Never before had players thrown two Pokémon into battle at once, and it felt like a natural progression of the battle system, allowing players to have two Pokémon whose types complimented each other.

Plus, this generation introduced new moves that were meant to be used during double battles. This gimmick has not changed since its inception, and it is because it feels natural for the series. There is nothing that needs to be changed about it, which makes it one of the best Game Freak has added to the series.

Why is it that I always forget that Mega Evolution is something that started in Pokémon X and Y? I always think that it was the gimmick from Pokémon Black and White. Tangent aside, Mega Evolution has become the most popular gimmick that Game Freak has added to the games.

It is so popular that people have continuously asked for more and more Pokémon to receive Mega Evolutions because the transformations are not only cool, but they are meaningful.

When Mega Evolution happens, it can sometimes change a Pokémon’s type, it can change the Pokémon’s ability, and it boosts the Pokémon’s stats tremendously. This can change the tide of a battle, but it isn’t so powerful that it is the ultimate trump card. It doesn’t allow you to blow away the opposition, but rather gives you more of a fighting chance and can dramatically help in certain situations. To this day, there are still Mega Evolutions being created, and it has been the focus in some competitive games as well.

I've missed Pokemon's Mega Evolution mechanic, and it's going to be a huge draw for Pokemon Legends: Z-A players.

Arc Raiders has delivered a big new update that's very fittingly on theme, and it's not without new mechanics.

Arc Raiders is kicking off its last major event of the year. The Cold Snap update arrives moments from now, and it’s perhaps the game’s biggest since its momentous launch in late October. We’ve known about the existence of Cold Snap for a while, of course, but we finally have a solid idea about what to expect.

Cold Snap is made up of different components - including new content - that all players have access to.

As the name suggests, of course, Cold Snap introduces the new snowfall Map Condition. As part of this, maps will be covered in snow, thanks to snowstorms sweeping across them. For one, snowfall makes it harder to see enemies, but it also turns all lakes solid.

Staying outdoors for too long will cause you to catch frostbite, which slowly drains HP. Embark says you’re going to need to bring more healing items with you on raids, and it doesn’t look like there are firepits that could keep you warm - though staying indoors for a while will help.

Cold Snap arrives alongside limited-time events that will be available until Tuesday, January 13. The snowfall visual update and new frostbite mechanics are available on Dam Battlegrounds, Buried City, Spaceport, and The Blue Gate.

One of the new events is Flickering Flames, which comes with its own progression track of 25 levels. Content is, of course, unlocked using Merits, which are earned from XP in matches. The other event is the Candleberry Banquet Project, which requires you to donate items found on the surface (including Candleberries).

You’ll earn rewards each time, and each stage completed will reveal a new scene on the banquet table. Likewise, there are cosmetic rewards as part of each stage, and you can use it as a source of Merits, too.
